https://www.politico.eu/article/belgium-.text: A group of Palestinian students and researchers is unlikely to take up scholarships at Belgian universities this fall due to disagreements in Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s coalition government over evacuating people from Gaza. Palestinians are currently unable to travel freely in or out of Gaza, which is under Israeli occupation, although a third country can request evacuation of students and researchers. Countries including Italy and the U.K. have set up systems to help Palestinian students take up study places abroad. But while scholarship applicants in Gaza received offers in June to begin classes this fall at some of Belgium’s top universities — including the Institute of Tropical Medicine, Hasselt University and the University of Antwerp — Belgian evacuations from Gaza have come to a halt under the coalition government led by Flemish nationalist De Wever. Advertisement Advertisement The students’ case highlights the limits of Belgium’s pro-Palestine stance, one of the strongest in Europe — particularly when it clashes with the Flemish nationalist-led government’s anti-migration policy . Belgium has pledged to recognize Palestinian statehood, imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank and urged the EU to do the same. A spokesperson for Immigration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt, from De Wever’s N-VA party said: “Evacuations are the competence of the Foreign Office but it is true that there is currently no consensus on this within the government.” Anne Weyembergh, vice-rector at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, which is set to host two students and three postdoc researchers, argued that if other EU countries could organize student evacuations, then Belgium should, too. “Some parties in the coalition are extremely reluctant when it comes to migration,” she said in an interview. “We feel this very clearly when it comes to our international students in general and our foreign colleagues who must come and get a visa to take part in conferences and meetings.” Weyembergh is one of 10 heads of Belgian universities who signed a letter from the scholars to De Wever and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot in July urging the government to help organize their safe departure. The exceptional circumstances in which the Palestinian scholars have earned their places in Belgium have not, so far, yielded any offer of help from the government. Advertisement Advertisement The obstacles facing them are partly procedural, mostly political. POLITICO spoke to four of the scholarship recipients, who were told visas could only be obtained in person at a Belgian diplomatic post, such as the one in Jerusalem. Two of them have been able to successfully obtain visas with the help of lawyers in Belgium, suggesting solutions can be found even in Belgium’s rigid immigration system. But visas on their own are of little help. None of the students and researchers offered funded places in Belgium currently have any way to actually get there. In a written statement, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories said it facilitates and encourages the evacuation of students and researchers from Gaza at the request of a third country. Anneleen Van Bossuyt speaks during a plenary session at the Belgian Federal Parliament in Brussels on June 5, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images But a spokesperson for Belgium’s foreign ministry, led by Prévot of the centrist Les Engagés party, said there was currently no decision in the coalition government to organize any more evacuations. The department said it was “actively investigating” what could be done to help the students but that any decision on new evacuations would be the “responsibility of the government as a whole.” Two Belgian government officials, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the coalition was divided on just about everything related to Palestine. While Prévot’s foreign ministry says it is looking for solutions, the French-speaking centrist Reformist Movement party (MR), whose leader Georges-Louis Bouchez is known for his pro-Israeli positions , and De Wever’s New Flemish Alliance (N-VA) are said to be against further evacuations. “It’s common knowledge that if something gets stuck [on this issue], it’s going to be those two parties that are against it,” one of the officials said. MR and De Wever’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Advertisement Advertisement Skills to rebuild Salwa Abu Elhaj, a business administration graduate in Gaza, said the offer of a funded place in KU Leuven’s Master of Communication Sciences program was “one of the happiest moments of my life.” Abu Elhaj was inspired to pivot to communications by her experience pursuing her undergraduate degree under the stress of war and, eventually, famine. She observed how the NGOs that became a “lifeline” in Gaza struggled to get their message to donors and international partners. Resolved to keep studying, she walked for up to an hour in search of a decent internet connection to submit scholarship applications and attend interviews. Between Abu Elhaj and her fellow scholars are many of the skills Gaza will need to rebuild — doctors, virologists, computer scientists. Ahmed Alsalibi, who has been offered a postdoc position at ULB , studies how resource-constrained health authorities can use AI to efficiently dispatch ambulances to where they’re needed most. Zuhair Dardona, also handpicked by ULB, plans to research how the conflagration of war, displacement and infrastructure damage affects the spread of infectious disease in his home city. Bart De Wever and Maxime Prévot are pictured at the Belgian Federal Parliament on April 2, 2026. | Jonas Roosens/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images Those barring the students’ evacuation “are destroying dreams and preventing people who have ambition, passion, and a genuine desire to contribute to and rebuild their countries from pursuing their futures,” Abu Elhaj said. In their letter to De Wever and Prévot, the scholars said they fully understood that Belgium must maintain its immigration and security requirements. “We are not asking for these requirements to be waived. We are asking for a practical and lawful way to fulfil them in the exceptional circumstances we are facing,” the letter said. The European Commission has helped to organize evacuations from Gaza, but only for medical treatment. A Commission spokesperson said they were aware of the students’ case, but that any evacuation would be a matter for “the member states concerned.” Other European countries continue to welcome students from Gaza. Italy established a “university corridor” for Palestinian students in May 2026, allowing more than 70 students to take their places in Italian universities — although dozens are still waiting for clearance to leave . The U.K. has also established its own scheme for scholarship students from Gaza. Weyembergh said the universities had put these examples to Belgian officials who had cited “logistical issues” in the way of evacuations. “They say it’s impossible,” she said. “But it doesn’t seem to us that it is.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/pedro-sa.text: When Pedro Sánchez agreed to appear in the Spanish parliament’s hearings on the Ceuta migration crisis, he knew he would face a hostile audience. But Thursday’s session promises to be a political reckoning for the Spanish leader, with an emboldened opposition and increasingly distrustful coalition partners seizing on a police report claiming that Morocco played a direct role in last month’s sudden arrival of 72,000 migrants in the autonomous city in North Africa. The report has dramatically raised the stakes for Sánchez. With the prime minister’s credibility eroding, lawmakers are demanding to know how Spain’s security services failed to detect a hostile operation by a supposedly close ally — and whether the government knew more about Morocco’s role than it previously admitted. Advertisement Advertisement “This wasn’t a spontaneous migration movement, but rather an operation that originated in Morocco and was spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco,” center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said at a rally in Ceuta on Wednesday. “The government knew and covered it up,” he added, calling for snap elections. “They lied to our faces.” In the immediate aftermath of the surge, Sánchez described it as an “attack on the territorial integrity of Spain,” but insisted Rabat had nothing to do with it . He doubled down on that position on Monday, assuring the public he had “no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities,” and instead accusing Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group” of orchestrating the operation. But according to the police report, first revealed by Spanish newspaper El Español , Moroccan agents helped orchestrate the mass entry of migrants into the exclave. El País later published a page from the document with images that appeared to show uniformed Moroccan security officers guiding groups of people toward the beach from which they could cross into Ceuta. The document was commissioned by a judge investigating the surge and drawn up by the National Center for Immigration and Borders, a specialized intelligence unit within Spain’s National Police. Advertisement Advertisement In a letter to National Police Director Francisco Pardo, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on Wednesday denied knowing of the report’s existence and expressed irritation that its contents had not been shared with the top officials convened to manage the crisis . Justice and Presidency Minister Félix Bolaños said the government had only learned of the document through the press and declined to comment on it until it had been properly examined. The report complicates the government’s efforts to avoid a direct clash with Rabat, whose assistance is needed both to deport unauthorized migrants and to prevent future surges. Sánchez on Monday insisted the crisis could “only be resolved with cooperation,” and that “showing a lack of confidence in Morocco will only aggravate this situation.” Political reckoning The report has turned Thursday’s hearing into a much more consequential political test for Sánchez. Far-right Vox party MEP Jorge Buxadé on Wednesday urged Spain’s parliament to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution, which provides for criminal proceedings against members of the government in certain circumstances. “This was an invasion of our territory, an act of hybrid war orchestrated by Morocco,” he said. “And this report shows the government knew about it beforehand and did nothing to stop it.” Advertisement Advertisement Demands for accountability are also now coming from Sánchez’s own coalition government. The junior partner in the executive, Sumar, has long questioned Rabat’s role in the crisis, and on Wednesday one of its member parties demanded Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska — who has always attributed the surge to human smuggling mafias — to step down if the information in the police report is proven to be true. “Not a leaf stirs in Morocco without the government knowing about it, and between 70,000 and 80,000 people don’t move en masse to the Ceuta border in trucks or on foot without being detected,” said Antonio Maíllo, coordinator of the United Left party, which is part of Sumar. “The Moroccan government’s involvement in the crisis is obvious.” The government’s parliamentary allies — among them the Republican Left of Catalonia and the Basque Nationalist Party — are expected to grill Sánchez on who knew what when, potentially exposing just how little room the prime minister has left in an increasingly uneasy coalition. That political isolation was also on display on Spain’s streets on Wednesday evening, with tens of thousands of protestors in participating in nationwide demonstrations condemning the situation in Ceuta. Protests were held in more than 260 cities, with dozens of Socialist mayors defying orders from the party leadership and taking part in rallies in support of the exclave. Their revolt underscores Sánchez’s difficulty enforcing party discipline among local politicians who increasingly see him as a political liability . With municipal and regional elections next May, the protests are a stark sign of the prime minister’s fragile standing heading into a crucial political year. Advertisement Advertisement
